summary:
Comets10: The Silent Fleet is a 22-page website that explains how 13 groups of NASA machines on the Moon, Mars and in deep space came to fall silent, from the Apollo Lunar Modules and Surveyor landers to the Mars rovers, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer and the Kepler telescope. Instead of sorting them by place, we sort them by how their story ended: they lost power or warmth, ran out of fuel, suffered damage or an error, or were left behind by choice. Each machine has a case file with NASA photographs, vital signs and a timeline, and a live silence clock shows how long each has been quiet.

The site answers the challenge by turning silent hardware into clear stories that explain why each machine stopped. It matters because these endings teach us how to design better missions, and they keep these explorers remembered.
details:
The Silent Fleet is a 22-page website that tells how 13 groups of NASA machines on the Moon, Mars and in deep space came to fall silent: the Apollo Lunar Modules, Lunar Roving Vehicles, ALSEP stations, Surveyor landers, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, the Viking landers, Phoenix and InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Pioneer and the Kepler telescope.

How it works. Instead of grouping the machines by place, we group them by how their story ended. There are four endings: they lost power or warmth, ran out of fuel, suffered damage or an error, or were left behind by choice. Visitors can pick a cause, then open any machine’s case file. Each file has a photo, a table of vital signs, key numbers and six sections: Born, Service record, The last signal, What it left us, Where it rests and a Mission log. A live silence clock uses today’s date to show how long each machine has been quiet, and a table compares each machine’s planned life with how long it really worked. For example, Sojourner was planned for 7 sols and worked 83, and Ingenuity was built for 5 flights and flew 72.

Benefits and impact. The site makes comparison easy. It answers a question that archives rarely show: why did each machine stop? It aims to help students and the public see that these machines ended for very different reasons, and that many worked far beyond what their teams expected. We hope it makes space history clearer and encourages curiosity about how missions end.

Data and resources. All mission facts and photographs come from NASA’s NSSDCA and NASA Science mission pages, listed in the NASA Data section. Every file links back to its NASA source page.

Tools. HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks. The silence clock and the filters run in the browser, and the site is hosted as static files. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write the code and the summaries, and we checked them against NASA’s sources. No images are AI-generated.

Creativity. The design looks like an archive of case files, with a paper-and-grid background, stamped “silent for” counters, colour-coded causes and bars that grow as time passes.

What we considered. We wanted a different view from a simple list of missions, so we sorted by cause of silence. We also wanted clear reading for non-experts, same-tab navigation with a working back button, and pages that fit phones and laptops.
